evidence_quotes.quote: L’objectif principal de la présente étude était donc de réaliser un diagnostic de l’alimentation en eau potable et de l’assainissement de base dans la commune de Kye-ossi.

Spécifiquement, il s’est agi de passer en revue le cadre institutionnel de la gestion des services de base d’assainissement et d’approvisionnement en eau potable ; d’analyser les acteurs de l’offre et de la demande de l’eau et des services d’assainissement de base ; identifier et cartographier les ouvrages hydrauliques et d’assainissement de base.

L’analyse du cadre institutionnel révèle que : les rôles des différents acteurs ne sont pas clairement définis et se recoupent très souvent. Il n’existe pas de plateforme de collaboration entre ces acteurs impliqués.
En zone urbaine, les données ont été collectées à travers un questionnaire administré à 200 ménages choisis au hasard dans la ville.
Seulement 26% et 69% des ménages de la commune de Kye-Ossi sont satisfaits respectivement du service d’AEP et du service d’assainissement.
Dans la commune de Kye-ossi (Figure 3), on a recensé 33 forages équipés de pompes à motricité humaine (PMH) dont vingt et un (21) sont fonctionnels et douze (12) non fonctionnels.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community access to drinking water supply and basic sanitation in the municipality of Kye-Ossi, South Cameroon, where there is neither a public water distribution network nor a municipal sanitation/emptying service.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2 (plain=yes) but fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (narrow=no). Under the plain wording, the study explicitly reviews the municipal institutional framework (Délégations of MINEE, MINEPDED, MINADER, MINSANTE and the Mairie de Kye-Ossi), documenting overlapping institutional roles, absence of a coordination platform, public versus private ownership of paid public latrines, water point management committees (COGES), and municipal financial/governance constraints affecting service provision. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, however, it does not empirically examine any rule-type legal, regulatory or administrative mechanism directly governing household access (such as eligibility screening, documentation or tenure rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, administrative burden, discretion or enforcement). Mention of vendor prices (100 FCFA per 20 L; 50-100 FCFA for public toilets) and non-compliance with technical drilling standards appears only descriptively within a general WASH infrastructure and stakeholder capacity diagnostic.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical mixed-methods data from semi-structured interviews with municipal sector officials and social institutions, rural village focus groups, a random household survey of 200 urban households, and a GPS-based census and functionality audit of hydraulic and public sanitation structures across the municipality.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports empirical access, availability, reliability and satisfaction outcomes, including household drinking-water source shares (40% boreholes, 17% wells, 6% springs), household sanitation facility types (33% improved pit latrines, 25% rudimentary pit latrines, 12% modern latrines), household satisfaction (26% satisfied with drinking water supply; 69% with basic sanitation), and infrastructure functionality (21 of 33 hand-pump boreholes functional; 7 of 7 modern wells functional; 4 of 4 private and 2 of 3 municipal public latrines functional).
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies the population and units of analysis (municipality of Kye-Ossi; n=200 urban households, rural village focus groups, supply/demand institutional stakeholders, and n=33 boreholes, 7 wells and 7 public latrines), the broad institutional/supply management context (though lacking a narrow rule-type legal/administrative exposure), the WASH access and functionality outcomes, and the cross-sectional mixed-methods diagnostic study design.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in French with an English title and abstract; per Inclusion Criterion 10, direct reading/translation from the provided French full text by the AI screener is feasible and fully supports methodological assessment.

study_design: Cross-sectional mixed-methods municipal diagnostic case study (household survey, rural focus groups, semi-structured stakeholder interviews, documentary review and GPS infrastructure functionality census)
population_and_sample: Municipality of Kye-Ossi, South Cameroon (estimated population 75,000): random sample of 200 urban households, rural village focus groups, semi-structured interviews with municipal sector officials and social institutions (schools, health centres, markets, religious establishments), and census of 33 hand-pump boreholes, 7 equipped wells and 7 paid public toilets.
exposure: Broad municipal institutional framework and stakeholder supply-management constraints (overlapping ministerial/municipal roles, absence of coordination platform, limited municipal funds, equipment/maintenance deficits, and public vs. private operation of public latrines); no rule-type legal, regulatory or administrative mechanism governing access examined.
outcome: Household drinking-water sources, household latrine types, household satisfaction with drinking-water supply (26%) and basic sanitation (69%),functionality of boreholes (21/33 functional), modern wells (7/7 functional) and paid public latrines (4/4 private and 2/3 municipal functional), and projected 2030 infrastructure needs.
rationale: Excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure) under the 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification of Criterion 2. Although the paper empirically assesses drinking-water and basic sanitation access in Kye-Ossi (Cameroon) and includes a descriptive institutional review of ministerial delegations, municipal capacity, coordination gaps and supply/demand actor constraints (which would satisfy the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2), it is a municipal WASH baseline diagnostic and SDG 6 infrastructure needs assessment rather than an analysis of a rule-type legal, administrative or regulatory mechanism directly governing service access.
